what_it_does: Post-quantum cryptography and fully homomorphic encryption (FHE — doing math on encrypted data without decrypting it) both rely on a mathematical operation called the Number Theoretic Transform (NTT), essentially a specialized version of the Fourier transform over modular arithmetic, plus very large integer multiplications. Dedicated custom chips (ASICs) run these operations orders of magnitude faster than ordinary CPUs, raising the question of how close a standard CPU can get. This paper first optimizes the code by hand for x86 processors and applies wide data-parallel instructions (SIMD — processing many numbers at once with one instruction, using AVX2 and AVX-512 extension sets), achieving 38x and 62x speedups over prior CPU code. It then proposes three new processor instructions called MQX that are specifically designed for the multi-word modular arithmetic patterns these algorithms repeat constantly, bringing the gap versus dedicated chips down to roughly 35x per core — and showing that a high-end multi-core server with these extensions could approach dedicated-chip throughput.
